title: Learning and discovery
thesis: In a roguelike the character dies but the player's knowledge survives, so the game is above all something to be learned: its design question is what players should come to understand, and how. The talks agree that learning must be possible from inside the game, through legible generators, feedback that lands near its cause and onboarding that does not interfere, but disagree about how much to hide: deliberate mystery, identification and spoilers are where a designer must decide which uncertainty is productive and which is just noise.

sections.heading: Knowledge is the progression
sections.brief: Open with the chapter's foundation: the heart of the roguelike is self-directed learning, and what survives permadeath is what the player knows. Show the convergence first: Andrea Roberts (deep self-directed learning as the genre's heart), George Moromisato (NetHack is about mastery across runs, not any one run), the 2016 lightning talk and Jim Shepard (the character restarts but the player does not), and Gillian Smith's argument that roguelike designers are educators who should ask what players are meant to learn, with her oatmeal model of agency, exposure and guardrails and her point that the lesson learned is rarely the one intended. Then the motivational side: Pandamander on anticipation rather than payoff, Hannah Blair Salzman on randomness and short runs making repetition feel like small tidbits, Ben McGraw on rich build screens letting players believe they can build their way out of failure (and learning the game meanwhile), Sersa Victory on mastering uncertainty, and Jon Perry's counterpoint that randomness can let players relax instead of optimise. Close with game-side memory of knowledge (Moria's monster memory inspiring Dwarf Fortress, Angband's monster dictionary) and slashie's caution that discovery motivates well alongside other elements but struggles to be the sole reason to return; end with guidance to decide explicitly what knowledge your game is built to teach and to give it somewhere to accumulate.

sections.heading: Knowledge, logic and wit: how players come to understand a game
sections.brief: Lay out the anatomy of roguelike skill using John Harris's three-way split into knowledge, logic and wit, and his account of how hidden probabilities pass from subconscious feel to conscious rule; his crossword and cryptogram analogy frames the goal of teaching what only experience can teach. Set this beside Pandamander's 'out of book' (generation forces players past memorisation into generalising) and Andrea Roberts on improvisation over rehearsal: three talks converging on the claim that roguelikes teach principles, not routes. Use Joel Clark's definition of chaos as the discomfort of trying to understand, his boss-pattern example, and his Blaseball evidence that players tolerate far more confusion than designers expect; pair bhauth's 'skill gap' lens (the difference between new and expert play is what the game teaches) as a practical evaluation tool. Add supporting cases (Roundguard's zones of likelihood, The Shrouded Isle's players learning what the systems reward, Tarn Adams on players learning to read clues alongside character skill, Gavin Verhey on data-driven versus intuition-driven drafters, the Sudoku constructors' shared meta-game) and finish at the far end of mastery: Kawa on conducts as the mechanics turned into a toy, Harris on NetHack's finite depth, and Tim Keenan on veterans preferring variety between runs. End with guidance: identify the gap between novice and expert behaviour in your game and design for that gap to be crossable.

sections.heading: Reading the generator: making randomness learnable
sections.brief: Argue that players can only learn from procedural content whose structure they can perceive; otherwise generation reads as noise. Lead with the convergence: Emilia Lazer-Walker ('black box emulation is indistinct from randomness', Computational Flaneur cutting sensors to GPS regions), Isaac Karth on the aesthetic locus (roguelike details keep attention on the surface) and on foregrounding causality, NetHack's sound messages and Minecraft's diamond rules as learnable generators, and Younès Rabii's framing of roguelike design as shaping player interpretation. Then expectation and surprise: Martin Pichlmair (delight is the gap between a rule-built expectation and the outcome), Max Kreminski (players need a baseline before exceptions register, and early random streaks mislead), Alex Byaly (correlated generation creates stereotypes whose rare exceptions surprise, and holding correlations fixed for a week so players can learn them), Matt Carney's In C parallel, and Nat Alison on flukes that turn out to be intended. Set against that the ways randomness miseducates: Rogue players inventing 'scroll heavy' games, Max Hawkins's apophenia, Evan Debenham on uniform ranges producing phantom patterns, and Shawn Main on randomness as an ego-protecting scapegoat. End with concrete techniques: tie generator techniques to visible signatures, surface causes in messages, prefer shaped distributions over flat ones, and keep some correlations stable long enough to be learned.

sections.heading: Feedback loops and the lessons of death
sections.brief: Start from Jeff Lait's problem: games excel at short feedback loops, but long-term consequences are among the hardest things to teach, and players who fail a long loop often blame the game; his cases are NetHack's hunger warning arriving too late, his survival 7DRL whose players never learned to stop and warm up, and Clair Obscur's nested loops as the good model. Set Lait's contrarian position (hard-to-learn games are a valid design space, and designers should sometimes break the 'everything learnable in a quick dopamine loop' rule on purpose) against the mainstream case for legible feedback: Sersa Victory's three conditions for meaningful choice, and Shawn Main's warning that heavy outcome randomness teaches the wrong lessons. Show the recurring novice failures that feedback must correct: bhauth on using consumables too rarely and too late, Josh Grams's players panicking in turn-based space flight, Nauticrawl's players not realising turns exist, Quinten Konyn underestimating a familiar weak enemy. Then present the post-mortem as the loop that closes long consequences: Kawa's expanded 'morgue' and its three functions, DCSS's exhaustive morgue versus NecroDancer's last twelve beats, Konyn's forensic reading of a morgue file, NetHack's damage-source tracking (Karth), aggregate player data on DCSS servers (Alan Malloy), recorded deaths encouraging in-character play, and map-keeping or keepsake play (Florence Smith Nicholls, Mike Cook). End with guidance on getting feedback to arrive near the decision that caused it and on making death explain itself.

sections.heading: Who is learning: genre literacy, player types and playtesting
sections.brief: Argue that much of a roguelike's difficulty is knowledge veterans no longer notice they carry, so designers must find and test their own assumptions. Converge Andrea Roberts (genre assumptions; Roundguard newcomers not knowing enemies hit back or that health spans a run), Tabea Iseli (game literacy like 'touching an enemy hurts', removing violence erasing it, borrowing farming-game harvesting instead of loot drops, and the balance between relying on and subverting literacy), Darren Grey (FTL's 'hero trap' and players treating trap detection and status effects as optional), Courtney Liessen's Reality Break players missing an editable rule, Into the Breach's deployment turn misread as random, and Alexei Pepers on expectations set by marketing and art. Then the first-contact problem: Ben McGraw's 'first five minutes' of build-and-die, Lee Tusman drawn in by a one-dimensional roguelike, and the different appetites for discovery (Lisa Brown's Gamer Motivation Profile and low-discovery preference for exposed rules, the Rise of the Roguelite panel on challenge versus story seekers). Finish with how you find out: Santiago Zapata's automap lesson (listen to players), Brian Cronin's playtesting that makes the game seem to read minds, and Max Sahin's warnings that asking players how they feel yields little and that general game research transfers poorly to roguelikes. End with a practical method: list the genre conventions your game assumes, decide which to rely on and which to subvert, and watch newcomers rather than asking them.

sections.heading: Teaching without interfering: onboarding, tutorials and complexity curves
sections.brief: Make the case that accessibility in a learning game means not interfering with learning rather than making the game easier or handing out answers (Andrea Roberts), and that up-front complexity is an investment the game must repay (Caelyn Sandel on Caves of Qud's front-loaded character creation). Then the toolkit, grouped by technique: short focused tutorials only for non-fun foundations (Roundguard), safety nets that trigger only for struggling players (Roundguard's skills reminder, Nauticrawl's diegetic safety-lock lessons after repeated deaths), premise-as-tutorial and wordless openings (Nauticrawl's stolen machine, Chogue's departing king, Bad News's mortician), tutorial levels and puzzles (Bloomquist, Shiren's Fei's Problems), quests that give lost players directed goals (Kristen Yu; Sandel's in-world survival-guide quest and Twine fan guide), curating the first experience (Shawn Main, Josh Grams disabling the first-level exit), and companions as teachers (Tyriq Plummer). Next, complexity pacing: Luck be a Landlord's rarity-gated complexity curve and Magic's commons (two talks converging on the same New World Order idea), UFO 50's gated microscopic scale, explicit synergy callouts for new players (Ezra Szanton), and choice-density tuning (Sersa Victory); set Jon Perry's deliberate maximalist overwhelm against them. Close with what happens when discoverability fails (bhauth on DCSS players never seeing most content, his ideas for archetype tutorials and unlockable mid-game saves, NetHack's wizard mode as a learning sandbox) and end with concrete rules for when to teach explicitly and when to stay out of the way.

sections.heading: Making the rules readable: transparency, common sense and in-world cues
sections.brief: Argue that whatever a player is meant to deduce must be deducible from inside the game, and survey the ways games achieve that. Lead with two in-world strategies: George Moromisato on NetHack leaning on everyday knowledge so interactions behave as common sense predicts (and the difficulty of that in sci-fi), and Mark R Johnson on Ultima Ratio Regum teaching cultures through clothing, architecture and speech rather than pop-up messages; set Jeremy Rose's caveat beside them, that a realistic simulation's simplifications are not obvious. Then explicit transparency: Bruno Dias's contract that Voyageur never tracks hidden state, Jongwoo Kim on consistent rules plus after-the-fact inquiry making unpredictable outcomes fair, Jim Shepard's 'guesswork is not gameplay', Angband's progressive monster recall and beginner knowledge menu, Brogue's in-game stats and flavor-text line, NetHack's internal encyclopedia, Cataclysm's in-game hint book. Finish with cues that hint without spoiling: Ultimate ADOM's context key with suggestive descriptions and auto-discovered secret doors, and trap design that exposes part of a hazard (Reed Lockwood's passive and active detection, Joris Dormans on never fully hidden traps). End with guidance on choosing for each mechanic between common-sense mapping, in-world cue, explicit statement and partial hint.

sections.heading: Known and unknown: information as a design lever
sections.brief: Treat what the player knows as a dial the designer sets, not a default. Lead with Nic Tringali: an unexplored dungeon is a shuffled deck whose contents already exist, and The Banished Vault inverts the usual model by showing every resource and hiding only the cost, so exploration becomes front-loaded planning and the real uncertainty is the player's own doubt and execution errors; include his warning that hiding the resources would feel like unfair output randomness. Set this against designs that build play out of hidden information: The Shrouded Isle (Jongwoo Kim on rewarding prudence with less information; Cat Manning on trait discovery as the core puzzle), Voyageur's one-or-two-fact destinations, Chronicles of Stampadia's shuffled checkboxes, Jonathan Lessard on limited awareness as deliberate, and hidden information as an alternative to dice (2016 lightning talk). Add small cases of concealment as texture: Brogue's hallucination, Robot Karaoke's hidden card names, Emoji Meadow's camouflaged animals, games' dowsing and treasure-sensing mechanics (Everest Pipkin). End with guidance: decide separately what the player knows about goals, costs and outcomes, and hide the one whose uncertainty makes the decision interesting.

sections.heading: System suspense: designing the unknown on purpose
sections.brief: Present the strongest pro-mystery position in the corpus: system suspense (a Caves of Qud team term, presented by Alexei Pepers) is moving through systems whose boundaries are not shown, so learning the game is part of the fun. Order: Pepers's definitions (surprise as a sudden change in the mental model, suspense as lingering awareness of a fuzzy region), productive versus unproductive uncertainty, the requirement for very clear communication everywhere else, and her warning that suspense turns to frustration when testing a hypothesis is costly (Baldur's Gate 3 patching the shovel; identification by use); then her three ways to resolve uncertainty, the value of content players only speculate about, and examples (Mass Effect 2's hidden counter, FromSoftware's many once-used secret mechanics, Caves of Qud's folk theories per Ray). Converge with Arvi Teikari (Noita hides rare interactions across many runs and leaves wand depth to experiment) and Courtney Liessen (revealing a 'fixed' rule can change delights players), and set Liessen's own open question, that signposting editable rules trades away the pleasure of finding them, against it. Bring in the deliberately misleading game: Leonard Richardson's call for mystery through secrecy or an unreliable narrator, robotfindskitten's symbol ambiguity, Joseph Hewitt on misdirection, Paul Dean on Pale Fire. End with guidance on choosing where to keep uncertainty, making hypotheses cheap to test, and keeping everything else crystal clear.

sections.heading: Identification: the per-run puzzle of unknown items
sections.brief: Treat item identification as the genre's founding discovery mechanic and the clearest case study of the chapter's tensions. Open with why it exists (Santiago Zapata: Rogue's unidentified items made a small content set feel larger) and the strongest case against it: Thomas Biskup removing it from Ultimate ADOM because casual players found it tedium and died with unused items, Slay the Spire simplifying unidentified potions away, and Lisa Brown on low-discovery players finding it work. Then the techniques that make it a game rather than a chore: NetHack price-identification and engrave-testing (Adeon), using prices as provenance or curse hints (Robin Mendoza), merging item categories into one larger pool (Eric Billingsley), how a starting identify spell transforms Advanced Rogue (John Harris), and Spencer Egart's mix of fixed intuitive and per-run randomised associations. Close with frontiers and readings: Mike Cook's proposal to generate whole rule sets so potions stay fresh, Alexandra Leonhart's Foucauldian reading, and the colourful examples (Kingdom of Loathing's per-player potions, Dungeon Court, the live-action roguelike). Cross-reference Pepers's hypothesis-cost warning in the system suspense section rather than repeating it. End with guidance on making identification cheap to probe, rich in partial clues and short enough to finish within a run.

sections.heading: Clues, riddles and research: discovery as investigation
sections.brief: Argue that discovery can be a deliberate act of investigation, with the game holding the answers and the player assembling them. Lead with Jason Grinblat's Caves of Qud library (cross-referencing generated secrets to narrow a location to one map tile) and its history learned only through present-day artifacts, then Mark Johnson's cryptic riddles (La-Mulana's gem scales, each puzzle demanding a new kind of attention, and Ultima Ratio Regum's unflagged leads trusting players to notice); add Tarn Adams on mysteries arising from local knowledge of a villain network and on townspeople whose hints act as a difficulty dial. Then fairness: Paris Buttfield-Addison's 'obtuse but not unfair' rule, hint buttons that point where to look, and deliberately unreliable sources to cross-check (with Grinblat's tolerance for misinformation that does not look like the answer); Andrew Plotkin on red-herring mazes, landmarks, losing your place and rule-discovery mazes; Bjarke Alexander Larsen on a dominant query-everything strategy and on perceived impossibility making players quit. Close with Alphaman's computer clues and Bad News's note-taking players and live-actor tension. End with guidance: every clue should lead somewhere, every puzzle-looking thing should be one, and solvability must be felt, not only true.

sections.heading: Spoilers, wikis and the solved game
sections.brief: Stage the chapter's sharpest disagreement: what to do about knowledge that lives outside the game. Set Brian Walker (the biggest threat to longevity is play becoming rote; optimal play should be fun and alt-tabbing to a wiki is not; a contingent strategy space only tips the odds) and the 'look it up' critics (Thomas Biskup calling required FAQs lazy design, Andrew Aversa on wiki-dependent difficulty, Moromisato's 'guide dang it', Jim Shepard on spoilers never being mandatory) against Jeremy Rose's defence of wikis as encyclopedias and discovery in their own right (with his Hitchhiker's Guide making every relationship visible), Drew Streib (knowing does not save you), Max Kreminski (don't fight it), and Grinblat's defence of a bug that sends players to the wiki. Show what defeating spoilers costs: John Harris on randomisation only delaying FAQs, Kingdom of Loathing's randomised puzzles solved by scripts, versus Caves of Qud's per-game disease cures recorded in an in-game book. Middle ground: Paris Buttfield-Addison's hint-line framing (what carries over is what you know) and his test of deciding which deaths players should look up and making sure the answer exists in the game; Angband's outdated 1996 guide; Nic Tringali on players optimising the fun out once a game is too well known. End with guidance: choose which knowledge you expect players to find outside, put a path to it inside, and keep the strategy space contingent enough that looking it up is not the optimal play.
